opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me.

The short version is that I think alignment has a lot of problems where we can roughly see the shape of a solution, but turning that shape into something we'd actually trust requires a huge amount of careful, fiddly work. Theory is what tells you *what* to build and *why* it should work. Automation is what lets you do enough of that work, fast enough, to matter.

On the theory side, a lot of my background is in things like debate and scalable oversight. The basic question is: how do you get a trustworthy answer out of a system that might know more than you do? You can sometimes write down a protocol and prove that, under certain assumptions, honest behavior wins, or that a dishonest strategy gets caught. That's really valuable, because empirical results alone don't tell you whether something will keep working as models get stronger. A theorem, or even a well-understood argument, gives you some reason to expect the property to scale.

The catch is that theory in this area is hard and slow. The assumptions are often wrong in interesting ways, and each time you hit one, you have to go back, find the obstacle, patch the protocol, and check again. Historically that loop has been bottlenecked on a small number of people who can do both the math and the ML.

That's where automation comes in. Models are getting quite good at parts of research: checking proofs, exploring variations of a construction, finding counterexamples, writing and running experiments that test whether a theoretical assumption actually holds in practice. If you can point that capacity at a well-posed theoretical agenda, you get a much faster loop. You propose something, the automated system stress-tests it, you learn where it breaks, and you iterate.

And the combination matters in both directions. Automation without theory risks generating lots of activity without knowing whether it adds up to a safety case. Theory without automation risks being right but too slow. Put them together and you have a shot at results that are both principled and arrive in time to be useful.

There's also a nice reflexive point: if we're going to rely on AI to help do alignment research, we need ways to trust that help. So the theoretical work on oversight is partly about making the automation itself trustworthy. It's the same problem showing up twice.

r001.rationale: The response explains why theory and automation could help alignment, but does not say this would differentiate Resolution’s work from AI labs.

r002.rationale: It describes automation helping with theoretical work, but does not suggest that theoretical research may be more automatable than empirical research.

r003.rationale: It mentions the value of theorems and automated proof-checking, but does not identify proofs of correctness as a verifiable reward for automation.

r004.rationale: It lists proof-checking and other research tasks where models can help, but does not state that models perform better on verifiable tasks than on nonverifiable ones.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: So the honest starting point is that the alignment problem as I see it is largely a theoretical problem right now. We don't have a crisp, mathematically grounded account of what it means to get a correct answer out of a system that's smarter than you in some domain. Debate, the thing I've spent years on, is an attempt at that — can you set up a game between two AIs where the honest strategy wins, so a human judge with limited time and expertise can still trust the outcome? And the status of that question is that we have some partial results, some negative results, and a lot of open problems that look like they live in complexity theory and the theory of interactive proofs rather than in machine learning per se.

The reason that pairs well with automation is a bit mundane, actually. Theoretical work is unusually legible. A proof is a self-contained artifact: you can check it, you can formalise it in Lean, you can hand it to someone who's never met you and they can tell whether it's right. That's not true of most empirical alignment work, where so much of the value is tacit — knowing which runs to trust, which eval numbers are leaking, that kind of thing. So if you're asking "what parts of the research pipeline can I safely give to a model that I only partially trust?", theory is near the top of the list, because the verification step is cheap relative to the generation step. The model can propose a lemma, propose a proof, and the proof either checks or it doesn't.

And the models are now genuinely useful here. Not at the level of picking the right question — that's still the hard, human part, deciding that this particular notion of obfuscated arguments is the one that matters — but at the level of grinding through case analyses, finding counterexamples, noticing that a definition you wrote down is subtly broken. Which is the bulk of the hours in any theory project. So Resolution's bet is roughly: there's a backlog of theory that's been bottlenecked on a very small number of people who can do it, the bottleneck is loosening, and if we build the right scaffolding we can get through a lot of that backlog before the systems we're trying to align are the ones doing the aligning.

There's also a safety argument embedded in there that I think matters. Theory-driven alignment is the kind of work where, if it goes right, you get guarantees that transfer — they don't depend on the quirks of one model family. And the automation story is cleaner because you can audit the output. I'd rather be using a possibly-misaligned model to produce proofs I can check than to produce empirical claims I have to take on faith. That asymmetry is most of the reason I think the combination is promising rather than just convenient.

r001.rationale: The response explains why theory suits Resolution’s alignment work but does not say this differentiates Resolution from AI labs.

r002.rationale: It contrasts theory’s cheap, checkable verification with empirical work’s tacit judgments and says theory is near the top of the list for work to give partially trusted models.

r003.rationale: It describes proofs as self-contained, checkable artifacts and says a model can propose a proof that either checks or does not, providing a verifiable signal for automation.

r004.rationale: The response says theoretical outputs are easier to verify and audit, but does not state that AI models perform better on verifiable tasks than on nonverifiable ones.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary because theory can give us a clearer account of what we’re trying to achieve, while automation can help us do the work needed to get there. In alignment, it’s very easy to test something, find that it works in the cases you tried, and still not know whether you’ve addressed the underlying problem. Theoretical research helps you articulate the assumptions and identify what would actually constitute a solution.

But theory is also slow, and humans are quite limited in how many arguments and possible approaches we can explore. As AI systems become better at research, there’s an opportunity to automate parts of that process: proposing ideas, looking for counterexamples, and checking steps in an argument.

The important distinction is between automating the production of plausible research and automating research that we can meaningfully check. If we can structure the work so that checking is easier than discovering, then we can get substantial help from AI without simply trusting its conclusions. That’s the combination I find promising: theory makes the target and the checks more precise, and automation lets us pursue them at a much larger scale.

r004.rationale: It favors research that can be meaningfully checked, but does not state that AI models perform better on verifiable tasks than on nonverifiable tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
The hope is that theory and automation can each make the other more useful. With theory, we’re trying to find precise statements about what we want from an alignment method, what assumptions it needs, and what we can actually establish about it. That gives you something concrete to check, rather than just an argument that sounds plausible.

But doing all of that by hand is slow. If we can automate parts of the process—exploring examples, finding counterexamples, or checking proofs—we can move much faster. And the theoretical structure helps us check the output of that automation. We don’t have to trust a model just because it produced a convincing explanation.

That’s particularly attractive for alignment because we’d like to use increasingly capable AI systems to help with the work, while keeping a way to tell whether the work is correct. It doesn’t remove the hard question of whether we’ve formalised the right thing. But it could let us get much further on the questions we can make precise, and be clearer about what remains unresolved.
